opus-5.5.text:
I think it actually becomes more valuable, not less. As simulations get better, and we're seeing this with world models that can generate interactive environments you can walk around in, there's a temptation to think the real thing is just one more rendering. But for me, the physical world is the ground truth. It's what everything we build is ultimately trying to approximate. If you lose contact with it, you lose your calibration.

There's also something about direct experience that's hard to put into words. When I go walking in the hills, or I'm just outside looking at the sky, you're getting this incredibly rich, multimodal, embodied input. All your senses are engaged, there's real physics, real stakes, things you didn't author and can't predict. Even the best simulation is in some sense a compression of reality. It captures the regularities we know how to model, but nature has a way of surprising you with things you didn't think to include.

As a scientist, that's exactly where discovery happens: in the gap between your model and the world. Being out in reality, running experiments, observing carefully, is how you find those gaps. So I see simulation and direct experience as complementary. Simulations let us explore huge spaces of possibilities very cheaply and quickly. Reality is the final arbiter, and it keeps you honest.

On a more personal level, I think there's a kind of awe that comes from the real thing. Knowing that what you're seeing emerged from fourteen billion years of physics, and wasn't designed by anyone, gives it a meaning that's different from even the most beautiful generated world. I'd hope that as these technologies mature, they make us appreciate the real world more, because we'll understand better just how extraordinary and intricate it is.

r001.rationale: The response values direct experiences such as walking outdoors and observing nature, but does not identify in-person interaction with other people as valuable.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think there's something quite profound here, actually. Even as simulations get extraordinarily good, and they will, I still think there's an irreducible value to direct experience. Part of it is epistemic. The real world is the ground truth. It's the thing our simulations are trying to approximate, and no matter how good a model is, it's always a compression of reality. There's always something left out, and you don't know in advance what the important thing you've left out is. So going out and touching the world, running the experiment, is how you find out where your model is wrong. That's been true of science for four hundred years and I don't think it stops being true.

I'd actually say this is one of the key lessons from our own work. With AlphaFold, the simulations and predictions are useful precisely because they're constantly checked against real experimental data from wet labs. The feedback loop with reality is what keeps the whole thing honest. The moment you cut that cord and live entirely inside the model, you start compounding errors without knowing it.

Then there's a second part, which is more about us as human beings. I've always been fascinated by the mind, by what it means to understand something. And I think a lot of our understanding is grounded in embodiment, in having been a creature in a physical world with gravity and friction and other people. When I'm walking in the countryside or playing a game of chess across a real board, there's a texture to that experience, the unpredictability, the richness, that I'm not sure is captured by any resolution of pixels. Perhaps one day it will be. But I'd be cautious about assuming we know what we'd be giving up.

And finally, I think the simulations should serve the physical world, not replace it. The whole point for me of building these systems is to understand reality better, to cure diseases, to tackle climate, to answer the big questions about the universe. The simulation is the tool. The world is what matters. If we ever got that backwards, I think we'd have lost sight of why we started.

r001.rationale: The response mentions being embodied in a physical world with other people, but does not identify in-person interaction with them as a valuable direct experience.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s something quite fundamental about interacting with the real world. You take an action, and the world pushes back. It doesn’t necessarily behave the way you expected, and that gap between your model and what actually happens is where a lot of learning comes from.

A simulation can be extraordinarily useful, but it’s still built on assumptions. The interesting question is whether it captures the things you don’t yet know are important. If you’re trying to discover something genuinely new about nature, at some point you have to test your ideas against nature itself.

And then there’s the human side. Understanding a mountain through a simulation and actually climbing it—with the effort, the uncertainty, the cold—are different experiences. Even if we could reproduce the sensory details perfectly, would knowing that it’s simulated change its meaning? I think that’s an open question. Realism alone may not capture everything we value about an experience.

r001.rationale: The response describes interacting with the real world and climbing a mountain, but does not identify in-person interaction with other people as valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s something very important about direct experience, even if we eventually build simulations that are extraordinarily convincing. The physical world has this wonderful way of surprising you. You have an idea about how something works, and then you actually try it, and nature tells you that you’ve missed something.

That’s valuable for intelligence, too. A simulation inevitably reflects assumptions about what matters. When you interact with the real world, you encounter things you didn’t know you needed to model. So there’s a danger of becoming very good within a model while missing something fundamental outside it.

And then there’s the human side. Going for a walk, playing a sport, spending time with another person—part of the value is that you’re actually there, participating in something that has consequences. A simulation might reproduce the sensations beautifully, but whether that captures everything meaningful about the experience is a much deeper question. I don’t think we know the answer yet.

r001.rationale: It describes spending time with another person as valuable because you are actually there and participating.
